text: Thank you, Justice Quinn. May it please the court. Your Honor, appellant is requesting that this court reverse and render the trial court's judgment in this case because the trial court did not have subject matter jurisdiction over the inverse condemnation claim. In order for Hayhook to recover under a takings claim, as this court is aware of, the first element is that the state intentionally performed certain acts, and then those acts resulted in the taking of property.

speaker: brianquinn

You authored an opinion in 2015 on a plea to the jurisdiction that Cremwell raised at that point. The Texas Supreme Court has held that the state wears two hats, the state as a party to a contract, and then the state as a sovereign, and when the state is acting pursuant to a contract, it lacks the requisite intent to commit a constitutional taking. This case involves the construction of a water transmission line by Cremwell across the Hayhook Ranch, and that occurred in 2009 timeframe. Going back a couple years in 2000, Cremwell had entered into a rather lengthy agreement concerning the installation of a water well field. I'll refer to that as the 2000 agreement. That was entered with the Campbells. Hayhook is a successor in interest to that agreement. In 2013, Hayhook brought suit against Cremwell, alleging that the construction of this pipeline both breached the 2000 agreement and asserted a claim for inverse condemnation. The plea to the jurisdiction on the breach of contract claim went up to this court. Ms. Quinn, you authored a well-reasoned opinion applying law...

speaker: brianquinn
text: Is that because they won?

Part of that agreement provided, and it was SPS that entered that agreement were the successor and interest, but access to water well sites and all easements reasonably necessary and desirable to develop the water rights.

At trial, Cremwell presented extensive evidence that it was operating pursuant to those agreements. speaker: brianquinn

speaker: timwilliams
text: No, Your Honor. However, I think based on the, I think what the court, the court could decide this just based on solely looking at the allegations made by Hayhook in their petition. In the petition, there's an acknowledgement of the contract. There's an assertion of a breach of contract claim under the 2000 agreement, the six damages under the 2000 agreement at trial. The parties entered stipulations that would provide for the calculation of damages. This formula, there's a, let me back up. And, you know, at trial, Hayhook requested the court enter judgment for a breach of contract claim in the alternative. So I want to look at some of the case law on point. The first case really that I think addresses this point of the color of right doctrine is the little text case of the Texas Supreme Court. And that was a consolidation of two cases. That's where the court said that, you know, essentially the state wears two hats. When you have your party to a contract hat on, you do not have the requisite intent to commit a constitutional taking. And I think this is important. Then Justice Abbott at the time, he wrote a concurring opinion. In his concurring opinion, he indicated he would add a requirement that there needs to be some additional finding that the state, you know, had a good faith belief that its actions were justified under the contract. The Texas Supreme Court has discussed this issue two more times. I think in 2007 and 2010, there's the State v. Holland case and the Kirby Lake case. And in neither of those cases did the Texas Supreme Court adopt this good faith requirement that Justice Abbott suggested at the time. And so that's why I think you can actually decide this based on Hayhook's claims in its petition and the acknowledgment of the existence of the contract.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Do those cases you mentioned or any other cases discuss the need for a relationship between the contract and the underlying dispute? Or can the state just say, hey, you know, this contract to purchase a car dealt with buying the airplane?

speaker: timwilliams
text: Well, there are a couple of cases. I think the State v. Holland may come pretty close to that scenario that you're discussing. There the GLO was working on a pollution abatement. The GLO contracted with two companies to provide services for a water processing facility. The plaintiff was actually a manager of one of those two companies. And the plaintiff built this filter system for the plants that was eventually adopted and placed in three filtration systems. After that, the plaintiff in his individual capacity, he went and applied for a patent on this filter technology and then turned around and looked at the state and said, well, hey, you owe me money for patent infringement royalties. And so the plaintiff's claim in that case was actually separate and outside of the contract with the two companies the GLO had contracted with. Irregardless, the state or the court in Holland said the absence of an express contract between Holland and the state or uncertainties about the existence of an implied contract between them are immaterial to determining the capacity in which the state is acting. And so really the focus should be, well, what did the state, were they acting pursuant to the contract? And so there doesn't, I mean, there needs to be some connection with the contract. But in the Holland case, the plaintiff wasn't even actually a party to the contract. I want to touch on a couple of things. The trial court did make a determination that the construction of this line fell outside of the scope of the 2000 agreement. The parties had interpretation disputes regarding whether this pipeline was allowed under the agreement. Trial court eventually determined that it was not. I don't think for purposes of whether the trial court had jurisdiction over the inverse condemnation claim, I don't think that's material. There's the Galveston-Whorst case out of the Houston Court of Appeals in 2009. And that case mirrors what we have here, where the government had leased some property and over the course of a couple of years, I think, had gone back to the plaintiff and got amendments to the lease agreement to provide for the construction of additional pedestrian walkways as well as that issue. One point the government went back and said, hey, I want to build more pedestrian walkways. The plaintiff said no. Government went ahead and did the construction of the pedestrian walkways. And the government said, well, I was acting pursuant to my rights under this lease agreement. Even though there had been an attempt to modify the agreement, so touching on the concern you raised earlier, you know, in the Galveston-Whorst case, they also tried to amend the agreement. The Court of Appeals in that case said, we do not decide which party's interpretation is correct to assess the trial court's subject matter jurisdiction over the suit. Even if the Whorst contract interpretation is incorrect, that would not change the capacity in which the government is acting. So the fact that the trial court here determined that the construction of this pipeline fell outside of the scope of the 2000 agreement, that's actually immaterial to whether the court had jurisdiction over the inverse condemnation claim. I did want to touch on some cases that Hayhook has raised just to draw a distinction. They've raised a couple lines of cases for the argument that, well, we know that Cremwell was intentionally building this pipeline. I mean, they had construction plans, they contacted landowners, and so that was an intentional act, and the intentional act of constructing the pipeline is enough to establish the takings clause. That is in reliance on a line of cases that I've referred to as the Jennings cases. In those cases, and it's typically the same fact pattern, government engages in some act like building a culvert or a ditch or something along those lines, results in flooding a neighboring property and there's a takings claim that is asserted. And so those, the Jennings line of cases has only been applied to involve circumstances in which the governmental entity's intentional act is not the actual physical taking of the property, but rather the cause of a physical taking. And that distinction is made in the Cope case that's been cited by both parties in their brief out of the Austin Court of Appeals, 2008. The other line of cases that I wanted...

And what you see here is this is land right here off to the east of the Hayhook. And this pipeline, what we call the phase three pipeline, it goes directly. It's an express route to bring water from off the Hayhook directly to pump station 21 that's on the Hayhook Ranch. That line, there was no easement for it by any agreement. And it also, it doesn't intersect or connect to any other pipeline. It doesn't, it just goes straight to a holding tank at the pumping station. Well, if you go back to the 2000 agreement that Mr. Williams talked about, what you see is that that's one right that was expressly not granted by that agreement. And secondly, there was no purpose here of connecting the one pipeline off property to another pipeline on property. It just simply didn't happen. And so that's fact finding number eight by the trial court. They never challenged that fact finding. So when we came into this court and filed our original brief, our view was that had been litigated. The court determined that there was no right for this construction and use under the contract. And so we had no breach of contract action under the trial court's rulings. Then we were left with a reverse condemnation case. And so that's that's where we are now. Now, what they're saying, you know, they're not saying, hey, we want to come and they've never said since the inception of the project, we want to pay you under this contract. And frankly, to us, it didn't matter. Our compensation was actually good under the contract and it would have been a lot cheaper to litigate that. We wouldn't have had to hire an appraiser. But once the trial court made that determination, we have no breach of contract action if the contract doesn't apply. And so what you've got here is a case where there's no contractual right. They took our property and and now they built the pipeline and they're not saying, hey, we want to pay under the contract. They're saying we don't want to pay anything. We want to take your land and use your land. They've been using it for 10 years and we don't want to pay any compensation. And that the problem with that is you've got you've got Article one, section 18 of the Texas Constitution for adequate compensation. And you can't just ignore that. I mean, they can't just ignore it. They're they're a sovereign. They're under a constitutional duty to pay adequate compensation. And that's exactly what the court did.

speaker: brianquinn
text: And so if I may ask, and I may have missed it, you may have said it, but I missed it. Can you explain to me why the trial court said there's no breach of contract cause of action?

text: Well, if the contract doesn't apply, then in other words, if there's nothing in the contract that gives Cremwell the right to to build this pipeline and provides compensation for it, then we don't have we don't have a contract to sue under at that point.

speaker: brianquinn

Hayhook was very careful to say, you know, we'll let you use all the pipes you need to get water off our property and to harvest the water rights that you pay for. But we don't want our land to be used under these agreements to build pipelines, to transport water from offsite across our property.

speaker: brianquinn
text: And they agreed to it. OK, and you've read, I'm sure, opposing counsel's cases about acting pursuant to a contract and how they were to have as a party to a contract. Why wouldn't that apply here, given that there's a contract in your name?

speaker: johnsmithee
text: Well, just because there's a contract between the parties doesn't mean that that that our action is a contract action. And specifically, they once once a governmental entity exceeds the rights or the license that's granted by a contract, it's a takings case at that point. And a case in point is is the Callaway versus Parks and Wildlife case. Now, that was a case where down in South Texas, Parks and Wildlife wanted to dig a canal across private property for fish migration. And so they reached an agreement for that. But there was an agreement that said that it would not be open to to boating in that canal. Well, at some point, Parks and Wildlife decided they wanted they were required to open it up for boating. And so they removed the obstacles that had been built that kept boats out of there. When the landowner sued the court in the Callaway case said that because you may have a contract action, but you've also got a takings claim because the governmental entity exceeded its its license under the agreement. It took more than it was entitled to under the agreement. And that's the way it has to be now here. They're not saying they're not saying at all that they had a right under an agreement. They're just saying, well, we mistakenly thought we had that right under the agreement. Now, like I said, we we had no idea that we were going to relitigate the whether this was covered under a contract in this court. But based on their original brief, there was nothing in there that challenged the trial court's ruling. So we we assumed that issue had been settled and we were moving on to the issue of whether their mistaken belief that they may have had a contractual right would basically exempt them from the provisions of the adequate compensation clause. And that can't be the law. If it was no, no governmental entity would ever have to pay damages for a takings case.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Are you suggesting that there should be an element regarding the mistake and whether or not it was a bona fide mistake or are you suggesting some other viewpoint?

speaker: johnsmithee
text: No, I think it just depends on whether whether the the use that the state put was was a use that was within an interpretation or was in the contract as a matter of law. It if it is in the contract, that's basically a defense to a taking. They didn't take anything because they had a contractual right to it here. They had no contractual right. So they took this. So, you know, you get back into the to the Supreme Court case that that that looked at this almost this exact issue years ago and basically came up with the concept that, look, if if if that a public entity could take this this position, they would never have to condemn property. They just said, oops, we thought we owned it. And so we don't have to pay pay you any money. And that's that's clearly not the law. Crim was not the first governmental entity that's tried to do this. It's been done in a number of cases, but no court has ever no reported decision has ever allowed a governmental unit to take this position successfully. It's not the first time the cases are unanimous that you can't just say, well, we made a mistake. We thought we had the right. The other. So there's two things here. One is the legal issue of whether a mistake becomes an exemption to the adequate compensation clause. And clearly it doesn't. And the second is whether the trial court erred in finding that that Cremwell had the requisite intent to take this property and the intent that is required in the little. Well, the intent that is required as little text case makes clear is the intent to commit the act that resulted in the take. And here there's no dispute. They don't dispute that. They intentionally went out there, planned a pipeline and dug a hole and put a pipeline in our property. And they've been using it 10 years. And so this isn't the color of title type case. This isn't where the state is withholding a performance under a contractual obligation. That's what that's what Leach was about. Leach. The Leach case is one of the best explanations that that came out of this court. It's not where the state is withholding performance under a contract. The court, the trial court didn't give us contractual benefits at all that we had contracted for. Rather, what it did in this case is it just said this isn't under the contract. So it's a takings claim and it needs to be treated like a takings claim. The other thing I would say is that when when we are on the color of title issue, it's what the one thing I would urge the court to do is to look at the Callaway case, which we cited. But but it says that that if once again, if there is any if the governmental entity exceeds its rights under a contract to that extent, it has committed a taking. And that's clearly what happened in this case. One other thing I should mention, and that is going back to whether any either of these agreements applied. I mean, the first thing is that the original water rights conveyance agreements back in 76, all it gave was the right to to basically develop the water rights on the property. And this clearly had nothing to do with that. The tooth out to the 2000 settlement agreement said you could it says you can connect pipelines. Well, there's some dispute over what that means. But even if it means you can build a connecting pipeline, it expressly said you can't build it to bring water onto the property from outside the property. And secondly, this didn't connect this phase three pipeline, didn't connect with any other pipeline. It went into a holding tank that went through a pump station and then ended up in the main pipeline. But the main pipeline isn't even depicted in the phase one plan. So it clearly doesn't meet the parameters of the 2000 settlement agreement. And so when the trial court found intent, it was making a fact finding that it had the right to make under the evidence that was before it. I mean, it's pretty clear that I mean, when when Primrock comes in and says, hey, we just made a mistake, we thought we owned it. Well, that doesn't really comport with the evidence because, first of all, they provide us an amendment. And in the amendment, it says because the prior agreements don't cover the phase of what we're doing in the phase three pipeline, we enter into this amendment. So they knew this. They knew it all along. And then we didn't. But they did. And so they know the fate. They know it doesn't apply. They put in the agreement and they keep saying we're not paying you a penny until you agree to amend the prior agreements. Well, for them to come into court now and say, well, we all thought we already had that right to amend to run this pipeline without amending it is a little disingenuous. So, you know, there were a lot of other indications in the record where where the trial court had there was a fact issue here. And the trial court found it against prim law. And that fact finding is not attacked before this in this court. So under the law, it's binding on this court. And so with the fact findings that are in place, it's clear that this is a takings claim. Anything else, counsel? I think that that's that's it, your honor. If there's no more questions, just Perl, just Parker, have any questions.
